author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Wrong Kind of Hero
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
The trouble began when Aang said the festival arch looked a little plain.

It was a freestanding wooden frame at the edge of Lanternwell Square, built to hold winter lanterns without placing more weight on the ancient stone arches. Tamsin had measured it carefully. Danse had checked the joints. Pip had painted small signs explaining which path remained open during the preparations.

"Plain?" Maui repeated.

Aang looked at the frame.

"Only a little. Perhaps we could add something that moves with the wind."

Maui smiled.

That should have warned us.

Within an hour they had invented a plan involving twelve ribbons, six carved birds, a hanging model of a canoe, and a spinning wheel meant to symbolize the Threadways. Aang could keep the wheel turning with a gentle current of air. Maui could lift the heavy decorations into position without a ladder.

I looked at the drawing.

"How much does all that weigh?"

Maui waved a hand.

"A heroic amount of not much."

"How much?"

"Not enough to trouble me."

"That's not the measurement I asked for."

Aang laughed nervously.

"We'll check it."

They did not check it before beginning.

I was helping Mara set up the baking stall when I heard the crack. Not a dramatic thunderclap. A short, brittle sound that came from wood under the wrong kind of strain.

Tamsin turned before I did.

"Stop!"

Aang dropped the breeze. Maui caught the spinning wheel before it could fall. The top beam sagged, and one joint opened far enough to reveal the pale wood inside.

Nobody was underneath.

Nobody was hurt.

We were lucky.

Tamsin did not look grateful.

"Who approved the additional load?" she asked.

Maui lowered the wheel.

"I thought—"

"That's not the answer."

Aang landed beside him.

"We wanted to make it beautiful."

"Beauty doesn't hold a beam together."

I watched both of them shrink a little under the force of that sentence.

Tamsin ordered the area cleared. Danse arrived and measured the deflection. The hanging decorations came down. A sign went up across the path until the frame could be inspected.

The festival was scheduled for the following evening.

Somebody would have to tell the volunteers the arch wasn't safe.

Aang looked miserable.

Maui looked as though he wanted to pull the whole structure apart and rebuild it with his bare hands.

I wanted to comfort them. I wanted to tell them the mistake had been small, that everyone knew they meant well.

Then I looked at Pip, who had spent the morning checking clearances for people who needed the wider route.

Their work was now blocked.

"Who is going to explain the closure?" I asked.

Aang looked at Maui.

Maui looked at me.

"Both of you," I said.

They went to the notice board.

It wasn't a heroic speech. Aang explained that they had increased the load without permission and damaged the festival frame. Maui acknowledged that he'd ignored the structural limits because he could lift the decorations easily. They apologized to the volunteers whose work had been interrupted.

Pip raised a hand.

"Will the repairs be complete by tomorrow?"

Tamsin answered.

"No."

A few people groaned.

Maui opened his mouth.

I caught his eye.

He closed it.

The festival committee chose an alternative: lanterns on independent stands along the safe route, with the main frame closed until inspected and repaired. It would be smaller. It would also be something people could actually use.

That evening I found Maui and Aang beside the damaged beam.

Maui was holding the damaged ribbon wheel at arm's length like evidence in a trial.

"A brilliant idea," he said, "defeated by the smallest possible piece of wood."

Aang looked miserable. "It was supposed to look like the wind carrying everyone home."

"It would have, if it hadn't tried to carry the arch with it."

Mini Maui swung from his upper arm and pointed dramatically at the sagging beam. Aang's staff leaned against the wall, and neither man could pretend the damage was imaginary.

"Can you fix it?" Aang asked.

"Of course I can fix it. I can lift the whole thing."

"That's not a repair," I said.

"Well, it's a very *impressive* relocation."

Aang laughed despite himself. Then he asked whether Pip could decide what decoration still worked within the approved load. Maui groaned as if the plan were a personal attack, but he went to find Pip with Aang instead of hanging the wheel by force. He was still enjoying the idea of a magnificent festival. He was simply learning that the crowd's enjoyment didn't give him permission to break the stage.

Neither looked pleased with himself.

"We were trying to make people happy," Aang said.

"I know."

"It was a good idea," Maui added.

"Parts of it were."

He frowned.

"That isn't very encouraging."

"It isn't meant to be. You both promised something before checking whether the structure could take it."

Aang sat on a bench.

"I hate disappointing people."

Maui nodded.

"I hate looking small."

The honesty surprised me.

I sat between them.

"Then maybe the problem wasn't the decorations," I said. "Maybe it was wanting the crowd to tell you you were good."

Maui looked offended for a second.

Then his expression changed.

Aang stared at his hands.

"I used to be the youngest person in every serious room," he said. "People looked at me and wanted the Avatar to have an answer. Sometimes I learned to act certain before I was."

Maui glanced at him.

"I've been doing that for centuries."

I wanted to laugh. I didn't.

"You can both be useful without being impressive," I said.

Maui folded his arms.

"That sounds dreadful."

"Try it."

The next morning they showed up at the square early, without costumes or fanfare.

Aang helped Pip carry the smaller lantern stands to their marked positions. Maui sorted hooks by size and replaced frayed cords. Tamsin supervised the repairs. Danse checked the temporary wiring and made sure the extension cables didn't cross the accessible path.

I passed out tea from Iroh's new house blend.

Mara brought bread.

Toph walked over, tapped the damaged frame with one heel, and made a noise of disapproval.

"That," she said, "is what happens when two show-offs think physics is optional."

Aang groaned.

Maui looked as though he might challenge her to a competition.

Toph smiled.

"Don't."

He didn't.

The festival began at dusk.

The square looked different from the original plan. There was no giant spinning wheel. No hanging canoe. The decorations were modest enough to let the old stone arches remain the center of the space without bearing any extra load.

Children carried lanterns along the safe route. Edda sat near the fountain where the path was wide enough for people to pass without squeezing around her. Neri opened the celebration with a short reminder of the Closed Bells: the lights were meant to guide, never to trap.

Maui stood beside Pip holding a spare bundle of hooks.

Aang helped a child whose lantern had gone out.

Nobody applauded them.

I watched Maui glance toward the crowd, then back at the work in his hands.

He smiled anyway.

After the festival, he met me beside the fountain.

"Well?" he asked.

"Well what?"

"Was I heroic?"

I looked at him.

"You noticed the cord that was about to come loose, and you fixed it before anybody tripped. You helped Pip without taking over. You accepted the smaller celebration."

He waited.

"That was good work," I said.

He considered it.

"Not very heroic."

"Maybe you have the wrong definition."

He laughed.

I took his hand and pulled him close enough to kiss.

"Can I have a reward?" he murmured.

I raised an eyebrow.

"Careful."

He winced.

"Right. Terrible word."

"You can ask for a kiss."

He smiled.

"May I kiss you?"

"Yes."

The kiss was gentle at first, then a little warmer when I curled my fingers into the edge of his cloak. The night smelled of burnt wick and fresh bread. I could hear Aang laughing with Toph near the stalls, and the quiet music of Greg's guitar carried over the square.

When we parted, Maui rested his forehead against mine.

"I think I like the smaller version," he said.

"Of the festival?"

"Of me."

I held his hand.

We walked home through the lanterns, leaving the damaged frame roped off for the repair team.

It was still broken.

Nobody needed us to pretend otherwise.
